A.explanation: Ampere per second is $\text{A s}^{-1}$, whereas charge from $Q = It$ is ampere second, $\text{A s}$.

B.explanation: Since potential difference is $V = W/Q$, rearrangement gives $Q = W/V$, so coulomb equals joule per volt.

C.explanation: From $P = VI$, $V = P/I$, so watt per ampere equals the volt, not the coulomb.

D.explanation: From $P = VI$, $I = P/V$, so watt per volt equals the ampere, not the coulomb.

hints: Notice the coulomb is the unit of charge $Q$, so look for a combination of units that can be rearranged to leave $Q$ alone.
Recall the two key relations for charge: $Q = It$ for current and $V = W/Q$ for potential difference in joules and volts.
Check each option by rearranging $V = W/Q$ and $P = VI$ to see whether joule per volt, watt per ampere or watt per volt simplifies to charge.
walkthrough: Identify the quantity: the coulomb $\text{C}$ is the SI unit of electric charge $Q$.
State the governing rule linking charge to energy and potential difference: $V = W/Q$, where $W$ is in joules and $V$ is in volts.
Rearrange for charge: multiply by $Q$ and divide by $V$ to get $Q = W/V$.
Translate to units: unit of $Q$ = unit of $W$ divided by unit of $V$, so $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ J V}^{-1}$.
Check the other options: watt per ampere is $P/I = V$, and watt per volt is $P/V = I$, while ampere per second is $I/t$.
Therefore joule per volt is the only combination equivalent to charge. This is option B.
